title: Verb tenses and tense consistency
blurb: Keep tenses consistent, choose the perfect and progressive tenses for the right timing, and handle “if” sentences and active voice.
question: A shift note reads, “At 8 a.m., Mr. Diaz complains of back pain. He has not slept well since the surgery, and if the night nurse would have known, she would have called.” Which verbs are wrong, and what should they be?

teach.body: Formally, tense is the form of a verb that shows the time of an action: past, present or future, each in simple, progressive and perfect forms. Plain English: the verb is the clock in the sentence. Readers trust that clock, so it must not jump from past to present without a reason, and each tense must match the timing it describes. The HESI A2 tests consistent tense, the right perfect or progressive tense, and “if” sentences.

teach.caption: “She had left before the doctor arrived”: had left happened first, so it takes the past perfect.

head: Tense
Form
Example
rows: She was charting when he called.
She will have finished by noon.

teach.h: Simple past vs the perfect tenses
teach.caption: A finished time (last March, in 2019) takes the simple past, never the present perfect: “renewed it last March,” not “has renewed it last March.”

teach.h: Do not shift tense without a reason
teach.body: Pick a time frame and stay in it. “Jo opens the file and read the notes” jumps from present to past for no reason: make both opened and read, or both opens and reads. A shift is correct only when the time really changes: “Last year Omar volunteered at a clinic; now he works there.” Check every verb in a sentence against the time words around it (yesterday, now, since, by the time).

teach.caption: “Would” never goes in the if-clause. In formal writing an unreal condition uses “were” for every subject (If I were ...).

rows.label: The patient was lifted by the aide.
The charts were reviewed at noon.
The night nurse reviewed the charts.

teach.note: Active: the subject does the action. Passive: be + past participle, and the subject receives the action. Passive is grammatical, not an error; the HESI A2 may ask you to identify which sentence is active.

teach.h: Scenario: Priya corrects a shift note
teach.body: CNA and nursing applicant Priya Shah reviews: “At 8 a.m., Mr. Diaz complains of back pain. He has not slept well since the surgery, and if the night nurse would have known, she would have called.” The note reports a past event, so “complains” becomes “complained.” “Has not slept ... since the surgery” is correct present perfect. The if-clause of an unreal past condition takes “had known,” not “would have known.”

teach.text: Three classic HESI A2 tense traps: “has” + a finished time (“has renewed it last March”), “would” inside the if-clause (“if I would have known”), and a sentence that starts in the past and slides into the present (“She walked in and sits down”).

items: Stay in one time frame; shift tense only when the time actually changes.
Present perfect (has worked) runs from the past to now; it never pairs with a finished time like “last March.”
Past perfect (had worked) marks the earlier of two past events; future perfect (will have worked) finishes before a future time.
Past progressive (was working) shows an action in progress when something else happened.
If-clauses: had + participle for the unreal past, never “would have.”
Active voice: the subject does the action; passive is grammatical, not an error.

summary: You can now keep verb tenses consistent and choose the simple, progressive or perfect tense that fits the timing. You can also build “if” sentences correctly and tell active voice from passive voice.

A.q: Which sentence keeps the verb tense consistent?
options: Ana checks the vitals and recorded them in the chart.
Ana checked the vitals and records them in the chart.
Ana checked the vitals and recorded them in the chart.
Ana checks the vitals and had recorded them in the chart.
A.why: Both verbs are in the simple past, describing two actions in the same time frame.

whyNot.0: Shifts from present (checks) to past (recorded) with no change in time.
whyNot.1: Shifts from past (checked) to present (records) with no change in time.
whyNot.3: “Had recorded” says the recording came before the checking, which is illogical, and it clashes with the present “checks.”

A.q: Which sentence correctly shows that the nurse's leaving came before the doctor's arrival?
options: The nurse has left before the doctor arrived.
The nurse had left before the doctor arrived.
The nurse leaves before the doctor arrived.
The nurse will have left before the doctor arrived.
A.why: The past perfect “had left” marks the earlier of two past actions.

whyNot.0: The present perfect “has left” cannot be paired with a finished past moment like “arrived.”
whyNot.2: Shifts from present (leaves) to past (arrived) without reason.
whyNot.3: The future perfect looks ahead, but “arrived” places the events in the past.

A.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “Dr. Okoye ___ at this hospital since she finished her residency.”
A.why: “Since” marks a span from a past point up to now, which calls for the present perfect: “has worked.”

whyNot.0: The simple present cannot carry a span that began in the past with “since.”
whyNot.2: The past perfect would mean the work ended before another past event.
whyNot.3: The present progressive does not pair with “since” for a span from the past.

B.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The aide ___ the patient's blood pressure when the call light went on.”
B.why: The past progressive (was + -ing) shows an action in progress in the past when another past action (went on) happened.

whyNot.0: The simple present clashes with the past “went on.”
whyNot.2: The present perfect connects to now, not to a moment in the past.
whyNot.3: The future tense clashes with the past “went on.”

B.q: Which verb phrase correctly completes the sentence? “If the clinic ___ open on Sunday, Marisol would have gotten her flu shot.”
B.why: An unreal past condition takes the past perfect in the if-clause: “If the clinic had been open ..., Marisol would have gotten ...”

whyNot.1: “Would have” belongs in the result clause, not after “if.”
whyNot.2: The present perfect does not express an unreal past condition.
whyNot.3: “Will be” is for a real future condition and clashes with “would have gotten.”

B.q: Which of these sentences is in the active voice?
options: The flu shots were given by the school nurse.
The school nurse gave the flu shots on Friday.
The flu shots had been ordered by the clinic.
The consent forms were signed by every parent.
B.why: The subject (the school nurse) does the action (gave), so the sentence is active.

whyNot.0: The subject “flu shots” receives the action (were given), so it is passive.
whyNot.2: The subject “flu shots” receives the action (had been ordered), so it is passive.
whyNot.3: The subject “consent forms” receives the action (were signed), so it is passive.

C.q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? “Last spring, Keisha volunteered at a free clinic, where she greets patients and filled out intake forms.”
C.why: The sentence describes last spring, so every verb stays in the past. “Greets” jumps to the present; it should be “greeted.”

whyNot.2: “Filled” is simple past, consistent with the time frame.
whyNot.3: “Where” correctly refers to the clinic, a place.

C.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “By the time her shift ends tonight, Rosa ___ twelve patients.”
C.why: The future perfect (will have + participle) shows an action completed before a future time (“by the time her shift ends tonight”).

whyNot.0: The present perfect runs up to now, not to a point later tonight.
whyNot.1: The past perfect marks an action before another past event, but the shift ends in the future.
whyNot.3: The simple past places the action in the past, which clashes with “tonight.”

C.q: Which sentence changes tense correctly because the time actually changes?
options: Last year Omar volunteered at the clinic, and now he works there.
Omar volunteers at the clinic last year, and now he works there.
Last year Omar volunteered at the clinic, and now he worked there.
Last year Omar has volunteered at the clinic, and now he works there.
C.why: “Last year” calls for the past (volunteered), and “now” calls for the present (works): the tense changes because the time changes.

whyNot.1: “Last year” is past time, so the present “volunteers” is wrong.
whyNot.2: “Now” is present time, so the past “worked” is wrong.
whyNot.3: The present perfect “has volunteered” does not pair with the finished time “last year.”

reteach.title: The verb is the clock on the wall
reteach.question: Imagine a story read aloud while a clock on the wall shows the time. What happens if the clock keeps jumping between yesterday and today?

blocks.body: A story set yesterday keeps the clock on yesterday: walked, asked, wrote. If one sentence suddenly says writes, the listener thinks the clock jumped to today. The only reason to move the clock is a real change in time, and the perfect tenses are how you show those moves: had marks something even earlier than yesterday, has stretches from the past right up to now, and will have finishes before a time still ahead.

blocks.text: “Has” and a stopped clock do not mix: “has visited last week” is wrong because last week is finished. Use “visited last week” or “has visited this week.”

explain.body: Verbs describing the same time frame use the same tense. Change tense only when the time actually changes.

test.q: Which pair of verbs removes the tense shift in “The patient walks to the desk and asked for water”?
test.why: Both actions happen in the same past moment, so both verbs take the simple past: walked and asked.

whyNot.1: Still shifts tense, and the past perfect would put the asking before the walking.
whyNot.2: Simply reverses the shift: past then present.
whyNot.3: “Walking” is not a complete verb, so the sentence would have no main verb for its first action.

explain.body: Present perfect (has/have + participle) covers action that began in the past and continues or still matters now. Past perfect (had + participle) marks the earlier of two past actions. Future perfect (will have + participle) finishes before a future time.

Signal
Example
rows: She will have graduated by May.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “Kevin ___ as a CNA for three years and still works at the same nursing home.”
test.why: The work began in the past and continues now (still works), which is the present perfect: has worked.

whyNot.0: “Had worked” suggests the work ended before another past event, but he still works there.
whyNot.1: The simple present cannot carry “for three years” of past-to-present time.
whyNot.3: The future perfect looks ahead to a future point, which the sentence does not mention.

explain.body: Progressive tenses (be + -ing) show an action in progress. The past progressive (was/were + -ing) often sets the scene when another past action interrupts it.

test.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “The power went out while the surgeon ___ the incision.”
test.why: The closing was in progress when the power went out, so the past progressive “was closing” is correct.

whyNot.0: The simple present clashes with the past “went out.”
whyNot.2: The present perfect connects to now, not to a past moment.
whyNot.3: The future tense clashes with the past “went out.”

explain.body: An unreal past condition takes had + participle after “if” and would have + participle in the result. In formal writing an unreal present condition uses “were” for every subject: “If I were the nurse, I would call.”

test.q: In formal written English, which sentence is correct?
options: If I was the charge nurse, I would change the schedule.
If I were the charge nurse, I will change the schedule.
If I were the charge nurse, I would change the schedule.
If I would be the charge nurse, I would change the schedule.
test.why: An unreal present condition takes the subjunctive “were” in formal writing and “would” in the result clause.

whyNot.0: In formal writing a condition contrary to fact takes “were,” not “was.”
whyNot.1: An unreal “if I were” condition pairs with “would,” not “will.”
whyNot.3: “Would” belongs in the result clause, not the if-clause.
